html:
The Yellow River, or Huang He, is the second longest river in China, about 5,400 km. It rises on the Tibetan Plateau, loops north around the Ordos desert, cuts through the Loess Plateau and crosses the North China Plain to the Bohai Sea.

Its valley was a cradle of Chinese civilisation. Neolithic farmers of the Longshan cultures grew millet on its soft, fertile soil. The Bronze Age Erlitou culture, perhaps the legendary Xia, and then the Shang built their cities along its middle course, and the Zhou rose in the valley of its tributary, the Wei.

The river takes its colour and its danger from the loess, a fine yellow silt it carries in huge amounts. The silt settles and raises the riverbed, so people built ever higher dykes until in places the river flows above the plain. When the dykes break, the floods are vast, and the river has often changed its course to the sea. It earned the name "China's Sorrow". Legend says Yu the Great, founder of the Xia, first tamed its floods.

Two modern floods were among the deadliest disasters ever recorded: the flood of 1887, and the flood of 1938, when Nationalist troops broke the dykes to slow the Japanese advance. The Grand Canal crosses it on its way from Hangzhou to Beijing.
